subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: When a protein is used as a respiratory substrate, its amino groups must first be removed by which process?
options: Decarboxylation
Hydrolysis of ATP
Phosphorylation
Deamination
questions.explain: Deamination removes the amino group from amino acids so the remaining carbon skeleton can enter respiration.

questions.q: In the link reaction, pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA by which type of reaction in addition to the removal of CO2?
options: Phosphorylation
Reduction
Decarboxylation and dehydrogenation (oxidation)
Hydrolysis
questions.explain: Pyruvate is both decarboxylated (losing CO2) and dehydrogenated (oxidised, reducing NAD) before combining with coenzyme A.

questions.q: In phloem, the mass-flow hypothesis explains translocation as a result of:
options: Cohesion-tension pulling sap upward
Capillary action in the sieve tubes
Active loading of sucrose at the source lowering water potential, drawing in water and raising hydrostatic pressure that drives flow to the sink
Diffusion of sucrose from source to sink
questions.explain: Sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure and forcing sap toward sinks where sucrose is unloaded.

questions.q: The chloride shift refers to:
options: The movement of Cl- into red blood cells to balance the charge as HCO3- leaves
The active uptake of chloride during the Bohr effect
The loss of Cl- from plasma during digestion
The exchange of oxygen for chloride at the alveoli
questions.explain: As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of red cells, chloride ions move in to maintain electrical neutrality.

questions.q: Why does reduced FAD ultimately lead to the synthesis of fewer ATP molecules than reduced NAD?
options: FAD donates its electrons at a later point on the chain, pumping fewer protons
FAD carries no electrons, only protons
FAD is not used by the electron transport chain
FAD is produced only in the cytoplasm
questions.explain: FAD feeds electrons in further along the chain than NAD, so fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made.

questions.q: What is the NET yield of ATP from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis alone?
options: 2 ATP
38 ATP
1 ATP
4 ATP
questions.explain: Four ATP are produced but two are invested in the early phosphorylation steps, giving a net gain of two ATP.

questions.q: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a shoot, which is used as an estimate of transpiration. A key assumption is that:
options: Water uptake exactly equals water lost as vapour
The shoot continues to grow during the experiment
No water is used in photosynthesis or stored in cells
Stomata are fully closed throughout
questions.explain: The potometer assumes that virtually all water taken up is lost in transpiration, though a small amount is actually used by the plant.

questions.q: As an organism increases in size, why does it require a specialised exchange surface?
options: Volume increases more slowly than surface area
Larger cells respire anaerobically and need no oxygen
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, slowing diffusion
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases, so diffusion across the body surface cannot meet metabolic demand
questions.explain: As size increases, volume rises faster than surface area, so the SA:V ratio falls and the body surface alone cannot supply the cells.

questions.q: In mammalian muscle during anaerobic respiration, what is the key role of reducing pyruvate to lactate?
options: To synthesise acetyl CoA for the Krebs cycle
To regenerate NAD so glycolysis can continue
To produce carbon dioxide for gas exchange
To generate additional ATP directly
questions.explain: Reducing pyruvate oxidises reduced NAD back to NAD, allowing glycolysis and its ATP yield to continue without oxygen.

questions.q: The sino-atrial node (SAN) is described as the pacemaker of the heart because it:
options: Initiates waves of excitation that set the basic heart rate
Conducts the impulse to the ventricles after a delay
Receives blood from the vena cava
Prevents the atria and ventricles from contracting together
questions.explain: The SAN spontaneously generates waves of depolarisation that spread across the atria and set the heart's intrinsic rhythm.

questions.q: Some toxins inhibit ATP synthase. What is the most direct effect on a respiring cell?
options: Glycolysis stops at once
Oxygen consumption increases sharply
Protons accumulate in the intermembrane space and ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis stops
The proton gradient collapses immediately and the chain speeds up
questions.explain: With the channel blocked, protons cannot flow back through the enzyme, so the gradient builds and ATP production halts.

questions.q: Companion cells are essential to phloem transport because they:
options: Conduct water under tension like xylem vessels
Provide ATP and actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements
Store starch for the sieve tubes
Contain no organelles, reducing resistance to flow
questions.explain: Companion cells, rich in mitochondria, actively load sucrose into sieve tubes at the source, driving mass flow.

questions.q: Which statement about the role of reduced NAD and reduced FAD in respiration is correct?
options: They are produced only during oxidative phosphorylation
They are the final electron acceptors of the chain
They directly phosphorylate ADP to ATP
They deliver electrons and protons to the electron transport chain
questions.explain: Reduced coenzymes carry electrons and protons to the carriers on the inner membrane, feeding the chain.

questions.q: Where in the mitochondrion are the electron carriers of the electron transport chain located?
options: The outer membrane
The intermembrane space
The matrix
The inner membrane (cristae)
questions.explain: The chain of carriers is embedded in the folded inner mitochondrial membrane, the cristae.

questions.q: A small mammal consumes 10 cm3 of oxygen and produces 8 cm3 of carbon dioxide in the same period. What is its respiratory quotient?
questions.explain: RQ = CO2 produced / O2 consumed = 8 / 10 = 0.8.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is mostly transported in the blood as:
options: Carbaminohaemoglobin
Hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red blood cells
Dissolved CO2 in the plasma
Carbonic acid in the plasma
questions.explain: Most CO2 is converted by carbonic anhydrase in red cells to carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogencarbonate ions carried in the plasma.

questions.q: Fetal haemoglobin has a dissociation curve to the LEFT of adult haemoglobin because:
options: It is less saturated at every partial pressure of oxygen
It has a higher affinity for oxygen, allowing it to load oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta
It must release oxygen more readily to the placenta
It carries less oxygen overall
questions.explain: A higher oxygen affinity (curve to the left) lets fetal Hb take up oxygen from maternal Hb across the placenta.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.

questions.q: How does anaerobic fermentation in yeast differ from that in mammalian muscle?
options: Yeast produces ethanol and CO2; muscle produces lactate
Both produce ethanol but only muscle releases CO2
Yeast uses oxygen whereas muscle does not
Yeast produces lactate; muscle produces ethanol
questions.explain: Yeast decarboxylates pyruvate and reduces it to ethanol, releasing CO2, whereas mammalian muscle forms lactate.

questions.q: Why does a lack of oxygen quickly halt the entire electron transport chain?
options: Without a final acceptor, electrons cannot move along the chain and carriers stay reduced
Oxygen is needed to phosphorylate glucose
Oxygen activates glycolysis enzymes
Oxygen directly makes ATP from ADP
questions.explain: With no oxygen to accept electrons at the end, the carriers remain reduced and the whole chain backs up and stops.

questions.q: Ultrafiltration in the renal glomerulus occurs because:
options: Active transport pushes plasma into the Bowman's capsule
High hydrostatic blood pressure forces small molecules through the basement membrane, which acts as a filter
The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, lowering pressure
Plasma proteins are actively secreted into the filtrate
questions.explain: High pressure (helped by a narrower efferent arteriole) forces water and small solutes through the basement membrane, which holds back proteins and cells.

questions.q: Tissue fluid is formed at the arteriole end of a capillary mainly because:
options: Hydrostatic (blood) pressure exceeds the oncotic pull of plasma proteins, forcing fluid out
The low water potential of the blood draws water out
Oncotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure
Plasma proteins leave the capillary
questions.explain: At the arteriole end high hydrostatic pressure outweighs the water potential gradient created by plasma proteins, so fluid is forced out.

questions.q: As a proton gradient is generated across the inner mitochondrial membrane, where do protons accumulate?
options: The outer membrane surface
The cytoplasm
The intermembrane space
The matrix
questions.explain: Electron carriers pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building the electrochemical gradient.

questions.q: Insects limit water loss from their tracheal system mainly by:
options: Producing surfactant in the tracheoles
Using haemoglobin to carry oxygen in the blood
Increasing ventilation by abdominal pumping
Closing the spiracles using valves and hairs
questions.explain: Spiracles can be closed by valves, reducing the evaporative water loss that would otherwise occur from the moist tracheal lining.

questions.q: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria and microvilli because they:
options: Carry out a large amount of active reabsorption requiring ATP and surface area
Secrete ADH into the filtrate
Produce urine of variable concentration
Filter the blood under high pressure
questions.explain: Reabsorbing most of the glucose, ions and water demands abundant ATP (mitochondria) and a large absorbing surface (microvilli).

questions.q: The very large surface area of the small intestine for absorption is produced by:
options: A dense capillary network in the submucosa only
Numerous goblet cells secreting mucus
Villi and microvilli on the epithelial cells
A thick muscular wall
questions.explain: Folded villi each covered in microvilli (the brush border) massively increase the absorptive surface area of the ileum.

questions.q: Spongy mesophyll in a leaf is adapted for gas exchange because:
options: It transports water to the stomata
It actively pumps carbon dioxide into the cells
Air spaces between loosely packed cells provide a large moist surface for diffusion
It contains many chloroplasts for trapping light
questions.explain: Loosely packed cells with interconnected air spaces give a large moist surface area, allowing gases to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells.

questions.q: At high altitude, where the partial pressure of oxygen is low, the oxygen dissociation curve of a well-adapted animal is often shifted to the LEFT because:
options: Haemoglobin must release oxygen more readily to tissues
A higher oxygen affinity helps haemoglobin load oxygen at the low oxygen partial pressures found there
Tissues require less oxygen at altitude
Carbon dioxide levels are always higher at altitude
questions.explain: A leftward shift (higher affinity) allows haemoglobin to become saturated despite the low oxygen partial pressure of high-altitude air.

questions.q: In the Krebs cycle, the regeneration of the 4-carbon acceptor molecule allows the cycle to:
options: Produce oxygen for the electron transport chain
Continuously accept further acetyl CoA molecules
Stop after one acetyl group is processed
Take place in the cytoplasm
questions.explain: Regenerating oxaloacetate means the cycle can keep accepting new acetyl groups, turning repeatedly as respiration continues.

questions.q: Which factor would DECREASE the rate of transpiration from a leaf?
options: An increase in atmospheric humidity
A rise in temperature
An increase in air movement (wind)
A decrease in atmospheric humidity
questions.explain: Higher humidity reduces the water-potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the atmosphere, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.
